PREFACE
It has taken years of efforts in compiling, checking and re-checking
of our material before these are printed and came in the hands of
readers. My colleagues and I have. spent quite a few years going around
the district and collecting informations. I hope this comes upto the
expe9tations 0.£ readers as a sing\e best source of information on the
Mahasu District.
Considerable material has been \ collected over several years to make
. this a comprehensive reference book. In the words of Ibbetson in his pre\ face to his very famous Punjab Census Report of 1881 "A Census Repor,t
~s not meant merely for the informatiJon of the Secretariat; it is intended
to be constantly referred to in every office of the Province. The mere
re~ults would ill serve this end in the absense of an interpreter. It is of
bu't small advantage to cast voluminous tables oj naked figures at the

heads of District Officers, without at the same time explaining what they
rep'):esent, which can be do~e by no one. but him who compiled them, and
drawing from 'them the more important conclusion$, to which they lead,
which few w~U draw but he whose special business it is to do so". This
comp,reliensiv,e reference book has to be a handy reference book for the
Administrato;rs, Planners and Scholarp. It is not meant to be taken up for
'leisurely reading but to obtain some specific information. Therefore, it is
very neces~~l'Y that this should be complete, should be brief and should
be very relevant and precise. We have collected material from many
sourc~s- a~d many old records had to be consul ted and then checked and
re-checkeri oyer long period.
It is the, keenness of Shri Asok Mitra, rcs, Registrar General, India
to have guided us in' this work. His devotion to the Census Organisation
is only ma,tched. by his versatility and many of Us have only achieved a
certairr' degree of completeness in our work because of his interest and
guidance.!
Different parts of the volume present the vil.lage-wise statistics and
brief write-ups on Education, Industry, Health, Community Development,
Animal Husbandry and Co-operation. Apart from certain data, most of
the other data, particularly regarding village directory is collected by us
from r961 Census Schedules. I have heavily leaned on old records, files,
notes and reference books and have also toured this Pradesh fairly
extensively year-after-year. Mahasu is the District which has undergone
some very obvious changes. There are some good roads, hospitals.
educational facilities, agr.icultural practices have all given this District
surprises which many people had never anticipated. The interior and inaccessible areas continue to receive due attention.
In this book I have been assisted by devoted and hard working
colleagues. They have burnt their mid-night oil and have toiled on their
holidays apart of being to difficult areas over the Pradesh. And with the
kjnd help that I have received from the Government of India Press,
Simla, it gives me a great pleasure and silent p.ride to see this report
cQmpleted: This report should have been printed much earlier but for a
number of reasons beyond control.
Right from the highest to the humblest my colleagues and I have
received appreciable considerations. With well over nearly 50 publications in hand, readers would realise that it was a pretty. arduous and at.
ti:q:les seemed' back breaking. This was an opportunity once in our life
time and we were obsessed to produce something of enduring vaJue. I do
~ot know_ how far we have succeeded and leave this to my readers to
Judge. I hope my readers would find this of interest.
RAM CHANDRA PAL SINGH

Boswell:
Simla-5.

.J[ahao"U Distrid

Tl\~ district was named after Mahasu
Deity which commands the largest number
of followers in the area around Theog.

Physical Aspects
The district lies iIi the outer Himalayas.
Situated between 76° 49'30" and 78° 18'35"
East longitude and between 30' 45'55" and
31 42'50" North latitude, with an area 2,256.5
square miles.
0

Boundaries: The district is bounded by
Tehri Gharwal of Uttar Pradesh and Simla
District of Punjab on the East. North-East
by Kinnaur District, south by Patiala and
Bilasour. On the West by Mandi' and Kangra
District of the Punjab on the North-~est.
Configuration: In shape it resembles the
butt of a gun. The district is entirely hilly
except the Pargana of Doon in Solon Tehsil
which is 1,500 feet high. The elevatIon of
this district varies from 1,500 feet to 26.000
feet. The main ]?eaks are1. Chur peak in Chaupal Tehsil.
2. Ghanshal peak in Rohru Tehsil.
3. Hattoo peak in KUIJllharsain Sub-tehsil
4. Shali peak in Seoni SUb-tehsil.

River System: The Sutlej is the main
river of this district. It takes its rise in the
eastern peaks of Himalayas. Taking its
course through Rampur Tehsil, Kumhiarsain
and Seoni Sub-tehsils it forms the boundary
line of Kulu District of Punjab and Karsog
Tehsil of Mandi District. There are bridges
at Rampur, Luri, Seoni and Tattapani to
cross the river. At Some places the river is
crossed by Jhulas.

The Pabar and Giri ave the tributaries of
the Jumuna. The Pabar runs through Rohru
and Jubbal Tehsils and covers about 60 miles.
The Giri runs through Kotkhai, Theog and
Kasumpti Tehsils.
Climate: The district possesses a variety
of climate varying according to elevation.
SUll}mer months are exceedingly hot in
Pargana Doon in Solon and places like Rampur and Seoni situated near the bank of'the
Sutlej. In upper regionS! the climate remains
cold throughout the year. The winter months
are severe in upper Mahasu.
RumjaU: There are 18 rain recording
stations in the district. The average rainfall
during :958 and 1959 was 50.32 and 48.08

The outstanding featUI'e of the structure
of Shali area IS the Shali thrust. The trace
of this thrust is almost circular. Within the
area bounded by the thrust the general
structure is that of a dome, with the rocks
dipping outwards in all directions.
The rocks above the Shali thrust belong to
the Chail Series. Those below the thrust are
of a mixed assemblage consisting of the
ShaH Series, the Madhan slates and Sabathu

and Dagshai beds of tertiary age. As a'-result
of nearly horizontal movement, the Ch~il
Series have been forced many kilometres to
the south-west over the sterata that are
younger in age, so as to overile them as fiat
sheet.
Subsequent denudation. removed this
covering G,f older rocks in the Shali area,
exposing" the younger rocks through 'window' structure. Thus, before the formation
of the Sutlej and the Nauti valleys, the
Chail Seriep must once have extended
right over what is now the Shali range, as a
flat though slightly warped sheet. The above
mentioned 'wmdow' structure is named as
'Shali Window' as it is! formed due to Shali
thrust.
'

other out-crops. on the north-western slopes
of the Nauti Khad.

of the district is 3,58,969 persons. There are
189,046 males and 169,923 females. This
forms about 26.57 percent of the total population of the Pradesh. The urban population
of five towns namely Arki, Narkanda, Rampur, Theog and Solon is 11,760 persons, 7,499
males and 4,261 females. It means that about
3.3' per cent of the population lives in towns
and the remaining in the rural areas.

The People
The population is composed chiefly of
Kanets with an admixture of Rajputs and
Brahmins. The other ,sections of the people
consist of Badhis, Chamars, Chanals. Julahe, Kalis, Lahars and ReharS', which are
Scheduled Castes. Among thoe Scheduled Tribes Gujjars and Kanauras are in large
numbers.
The RajputSl form rather a ruling class
than a caste and comprise all the families of
the hill chiefs. There are three categories of
Rajputs. First is the ruling family, who do
not give their daughters to Khash. Mians or
other Rajputs. They still marry among other
ruling Rajput families. The second are

Thakurs or Mians. They also hesitate to give
thieir daughters to Kanets or Kha:sh. 'l;.'hen
there are Kanets who ~re mainly fl.gricul~
turists.
Brahmins are of two classes-Sasani and
Dharebar. The Sasanis are generally muafidar and are of a distinctly higher class than
the Dharebars. Previously they did not
admit the custom of Reet or transference of
wives to others on payment of money to
their legitimate husbands. They were indifferent cultivators. They would marry
Dharebar women but will not give their own
daughters in marriage to ,them. Dharebar
Brahmins uractise all the customs of the
Kanets. Other groups of the Brahmins are:(a) Bhcits: Who assemble at a wedding
or birth of CIt boy to exact their dues.
They sing Kavitas. They have no
connection with otiher Brahmins.
(b) Pandas: take the' alms given in the
name 0:( Rahu, Ketil and Sanicharthe evil stars.
(c) Acharnj a.nd Mahacharaj OT Bedwas: They are given no alms except those given in the name ot the
dead. They are not allowed to enter
any house except when a death occurs.
The Kolis form the mass of population
among SchE!duled Castes. In lower parts of
the district, the Kolis identify themselves
with Kanets. Other cast~s are Chamars, Jullahe, Lahars and Rehars.
Gujja;rs are both Hindus and Muslims.
The Hindu Gujjars have more or less settled on land and follow the plough. The Mus-lir,n Gujjars follow a nomadic life. In summer they move to higher hills in search of
new pastures and in winter they come down.
They form the floating population.

Thel'e is nD important historical place connected with Muslims, Sikhs and other religlans ei'cept ~Christians who have well
khown Church at Kotgarh.
The distrIct is covered by a net work of
shrines and 1IempEes. Almost every viUagle
has a local deota and a temple. The people
are mostly shaktiks and besides worshipping shiva also worship Durga. The temples
dedicated to Durga at Sarahan, Hatkoti,
Taradevi, Shali and Seopi are quite faanous
arid command a large number of devotees.
The ancient temple of Mahasu at Gijari in
Theog is also very famous and is worshipped by a large number of devotees. Symbols
of Gods are genera.lly of one type, though
they bear different names. The modes of
worship are the same and; therr images alike.
Some goddesses are represented with 2
arms, some wHh 4, some with 8, 12 or even
16. Some are shown sitting upon a dead body
and slOme as riding on a lion. Here and there
some temples may have images of Ganesh
and other gods and goddesses which may
be purely local in character.
Temple priests are generally Brahmins.
Some of them enjoy free grants of land as
remuneration for their services in the temple. They receive some grains at each har"est f~om every worshipper.
A common sacrifice is that of a goat. The
head of the goat is place(l before the image
of the deota for sometime. One loin is given
to the person who offered it and the rel1lain~
der is distributed among the Dinwans and
the priest.
Food and Dress: The staple food of the
villagers consist of maize, rice and wheat.
Wheat is taken mostly in summer and after
that occasionally. Pulses like urd, lobia,
moong and kolth are used either daily or
every third day. Chaili the lunch and Bayali
the supper are the two main meals besides
, the breakfast that is called nawari. In hot
weather satltus of maize flour parched before
grinding, are taken either with water or butter-milk. Bathu, Gauni and Koda are taken
specially in winter. Butter, milk and curds
are always used. Meat and fish are relished
by the majority of Rajputs.
Clothing: Cotton as well as woollen clothes
are worn. As the winter is severe, woollen
clothes prepared out of patties are used.
Ordinary clothing for men consists of shirt,
pyjama and a. cap. In lower Mahasu majority go without pyjama wearing only a small
loin cloth in summer and rainy season

Cap is more in use. Women put on Salwar,
Kamiz and Dhatu. In the upper part of the
district the traditional dress of a man consists of black woollen pyjama, coat and Bushahri cap. The women wear Pakhati, Kamiz
and a small Dhatu, Women of Rampur Tehsil
put on woollen cap and Giddi. The typical
dress of the women of Theog Tehsil'is Sal war
and Kamiz with Dhatu as the head-dress.

District Administration

The Deputy Commissioner is the administrative head of the district. He is responsible
for general administration and maintenance
of law and order. He is assisted by a Treasury
Officer, a Revenue AS'sistant and a Compensation Officer. There is an Assistant District
Planning and Development Officer.
The Judicial set up of the district comprises
of one District and Sessions Judge, two
Sub-Judges each at Tlieog and RohirU three
Magistrates First Class having their headquarters at Rampur, Solon and Theog.
The district comprises of 8 tehsils and 3
sub-tehsils, 18 Kanungo circles and 136
Patwar circles. Each tehsil and sub-tehsil
is under the charge of a Tehsildar 'and a SubTehsildar respectively.
The district police force is under the
charge of a Superintendent of Police. There
were 2 Deputy Superintendents of Police, 4
Inspectors, 21 Sub-Inspectors, 19 Assistant
Sub-Inspectors, 98 Head Constables .and 513
Constables in the district on 31st December,
1960.

The District Medical Officer is the controlling officer in respect of all the medical
and public health institutions in the district.
The District Inspector of Schools is the head
of office for Primary and Middle Schools.
The Headmasters are the controlling officers in respect of High and Higher Secondary
Schools.
In 1957 some departments were transferred to the control of the Territorial Council
.under Section 28 of the Territorial Councils
Act, 1956.' The departments transferred to,
the Council were Education up to Higher
Secondary stage, Medical and Public Health,
Veterinary Services and Construction and
maintenance of mule roads.

Education

The district has made substantial progress
in the .:field of education. The literacy percentage during the past decade has gone-up
from 4.6 percent in 1951 to 19.3 percent in
1961. According to 1961 Census, 18.01 % are
literate and educated in the rural areas.
Lit~racy among females is considerably low
WhICh stands at 5.96% as against 29.0%
aJ?ong males. However these figures are
hIgher than the Pradesh figures which are
25.19% and 4.62% males and females. In
respect of the urban areas the district figures
are pretty high as more than half the urban
population has been returned as literate and
educated. The literacy figure stands at
58.65% in urban ar.eas against 18.0% in the
rural.

Arki town leads all other towns. As usual,
the percentage of literate males is higher
than females but literacy among females
does not lag behind in urban areas by such
margin as in rural areas. Rural figures of
district for males are 5.96% where as 47.17%
females are literate in the urban areas.
The literacy has increased as a result of
opening of a net work of educational institutions in the district. Tables 7.1 and 7.3 give
an idea of the increase in the institutions
and scholars. In 1953-54 there were 10 high
schools, 40 middle and lower middle schools
and 262 primary schools which rose to 26,
40 and 342 respectively in 1960-61. There are
two degree colleges in the district, one at
Solon and the other at Rampur. There is an
agricu'lture college too at Solon. Similarly
the number of scholars has increased by 68
percent during this period. Facilities for the
education of women have been extended.
Now there are three higher secondary
schools at Arki, Solon and Theog and one
high school at Kotkhai for girls.

Government . College, Solon: To cope
with the urgent need of Higher Education
in Himachal Pradesh, Government Degree
College, Solon, was started during July,
1959. The following Courses of studies have
been provided in the Degree College:-

1. Humanities and Science
2. Pre-Engineering
3. Pre-Medical
4. B.A. Part I, II and III
5. B.Sc. 3 Year Course
At present 317 scholars are studying in
Government Degree College, Solon, out of
which 241 are boys and 76 are girl students.

Government Training College, Solon: In
order to meet the increasing demand of
Trained Graduate Teachers for Secondary
Schools in the Pradesh, the Himachal Pradesh Administration started one Government Training College at Auhar, but the
same was shifted to Solon during 1957-58.
The College is affiliated to the Panjab University. 75 percent seats reserved for in ser~
vice trainees and the remaining 25 percent
are thrown open for direct admission. All
the trainees are required to execute a bond
to serve the Himachal Pradesh Government
for 5 years. The duration of B.Ed. is one
year. At present 113 students including 34
girls are studying in the College.
Government Basic' Training School,
Solon: In order to meet the shortage of
Junior Basic Trained Teachers in. Schools in
this Pradesh, Government B.T. School,
Solon, was started during the year 1951.
These teachers are trained to teach the Primary classes in BaSIC Schools. At\ present
105 trainees including 24 girl trainees are ~
undergoing training there. During the training period they get their pay and allowances.
The duration of training is one year.
Sanskrit Pathshala, Solon: This institution
was initially started long before the formation of Himachal Pradesh. Its staff, building
and equipment underwent a complete renovation in the year 1956. The institution is
]IOW known as Government Sanskrit Mahavidyalya, Solon and- is affitiated to the Panjab University. It prepares candidates for
Pragya, Vishard and Shastri in Sanskrit,
Acharya, Ra1Jan and Prabhakar in Hindi.
At present 12 students including one girl are
studying there.
Medical and Public Health

There were about 18 medical institutions
at the time of the formation of this district.
These institutions were opened by some old
rulers at the capitals of the princely states.
Mala.ria, tuberculosis, gastro-intestinal and
comn!unicable diseases used to take a heavy
toll. Respiratory diseases mostly influenza,
Pneumonia and malnutrition were common.
Medical Department was set-up immediately after the formation of the district under
the control of a District Medical Officer to
combat these diseases and to afford relief to
the people. In addition to public health unit
institutions like maternity and Child Wel~
fare Centres were established at different
places during the Second Five Year Plan.

V. D. Organisation: The V. D. Organisation 'was started by the World Health Organisation, in May, 1949 at Simla. The V. D.
Clinic was attached to Ripon Hospital.
Laboratory and Office were established in
Hawthorn Cottage. In 1951 the V. D. Organisation was taken over by the Medical
Department of Himachal Pradesh. In the year
1952 the clinic was shifted to Snowdon Hospital. During Second Five Year Plan 8 clinics
were started at Arki, Bagi, Chaupal, Jubbal,
Kumharsain, Rampur, Rohru and Solon.
The V. D. teams conduct survey in the remotest corners of the district.

During the Third Plan V. D. Unit has
been opened at Primary Health Centre Kot·
khai.

Leprosy: Leprosy subsidiary control centre with 30 indoor beds was opened at
Mashobra in January, 1956. Now there are

five Leprosy sub-units functioning at Koti,
Narkanda Rampur, Rohru and 'l'heog under
the charg~ of Non-Medical Assistants or
Social Workers to give domiciliary treatment
to the patients in the respective areas.
Serious patients are referred to' the Leprosy
Hospital, Mashobra for admission and regular treatment.
Malaria: The Malaria Control Programme
was started in the district in 1953. In 1958
the Malaria Control Programme as switched
over to National Malaria Eradication Programme. As a result of mass spraying,. the
incidence of this disease has been conslderably reduced. 397 deaths were ~eport~d due
to malaria in 1952 and 72 only III 1959. The
disease is expected to be completely wiped
out during the Third Five Year Plan.
T. B. Sanatorium: In view of the high
incidence of tuberculosis in the district a 20
bed clinic was opened at Mashobra in 1951.
It was inadequate to accommodate the
urgent cases. Accordingly a T.B. Sanatorium
was set up at Mandodhar and the clinic at
Ma<:lhobra was attached to it .

Goitre: Under the goitre scheme, iodised
salt is distribmtted free of charge to the
patients for the treatment of goitre. This
scheme was started in the district in 1959.
Training: A Training School has been
started at the Snowdon Hospital for'the
Lady Health Visitors Course,
With the spreading of education and availability of more and more medical facilities
there is improvement in the general public
health standard. Instead of resorting to
witchcraft and jantar-mantar treatment
people avail of the medical facilities provided by the State on such an extensive scale.

Agrioulture
Agriculture is the main occupation of the
people in the district as it engages about 80
per cent of the working population. Most of \
the others depend directly or indirectly
upon it. As the terrain throughout the district is hilly and holdings are very small and
scattered, the yield of various crops is much
lower than in the plains and scope for increasing production is rather limited. Mahasu
district by virtue of its varied altitude and
agroclimatic conditions possesses vast potentialities for growing a wide variety of temperate fruits and cash crops like potato
ginger and vegetables.
'

16
Major food crops are grouped in three
categories viz., cereals, pulses and other food
crops. Non-food crops are divided into two
sectors ofloil seeds and other non-food crops
such as cotton, tobacco and fodder.

Crops: As in the other parts of 'the Pradesh there are two agricultural seaSOns,
n~mely Kharif and Rabi. Rice, maize, millets, ragi and pulses are the main crops
~rown in Kharif season. Wheat, baTle~ and
gram are grown in Rabi season. In addition,
the district has earned a name for itself as
a producer and supplier of high quality
apples and seed potatoes.

Horticultural Wo'rks: In 1920 an American
Missionary, Mir. S. Stokes, started fruit cultivation in Kotgarh with "delicious" varieties
of apple which are now widely grown. With
the advent of Five Year Plans, a concerted drive was launched to focus the
attention of the farmers on fruit production.
Varied altitudes and agro-climatic conditions of the district afford potentialities for
grc.wing different fruits from sub-tropical
like citrus and even mango in the valley
areas to temperate, like apple and cherry
in high hills. Besides distribution of temperate and sub-tropical fruit plants through
the extension staff the horticultural staff
remains busy in pruning, budding, grafting
and other such activities which go a long
way in the development of orchards for
which the district is ideally suited. Horticultural loans at the rate of Rs. 500 per acre
are being sanctioned to the cultivators. 16

Plant Protection work in the District:
Under this scheme necessary gUidance and
help is given to the cultivators in combating
pests and diseases of fruits, vegetables and
crops. Pesticides are also supplied to the
farmers at subsidised rates. Plant protection
equipment is given to the cultivators at 50%
subsidised rates. The technical guidance in
respect of various operations fixation of targets of work, arrangement for supply of
plant p'rotection equipment and pesticides
was rendered by the District Agricultural
Officer with the help of the Plant Proteation
Assistant in the district. B'esides this, there
are three Plant Protection Sub-Centres in
the district locateq at Thanedhar, Kotkhai
and Tikkar and these were established in
the year, 1958 arid 1962. Besides, there are
Research Centres, Schools, Colleges and
Model Farms in the district. The detail for
all these is as under:I

(1) Crop and Vegetable Research Station,
Solon: There is one crop and vegetable research station at Solon which
was established in the year, 1958.
T~e research! work, comprising 'trials
wltb local aug e~Qtic v~rieties of

19
wheat, barley, and black gram with
a view of evolving suitable varieties
for different areas, is in progress.
Vegetable seeds grown in hilly area
are multiplied at this statiop. Sliitability of different varieties is also
worked out at this station.
(2) Vocational
Agricultural
School
'Chharabra: It is located at Chharabra near Mashobra. It imparts
training in agriculture to new entrants for which minimum qualification is matriculate. The school has
now been shifted to Kotkhai and
Dhaulakuan where half the number
of trainees is traIned in temperate
and sub!.tropical conditions.
(3) Regi'pnat Fruit Research Station,
Mashobra: The Fruit Research Station, \ Mashobra started towards the
I end of 1953
and was raised to the
statu~ of Regional Fruit Research
Stati~n for temperate fruits in the
year, 1958 by providing more staff
and funds. It is the first Regional
Fruit Research Station to be establishled in the country and would
cater to the needs of the Northern
hilly,areas for temperate fruits. The
Regional Station came into being
with the establishment of three sections, Pomology, Entomology and
Nycology. At the beginning of the
Third Five Year Plan, three more
sections, Fruit Breeding, Physiology
and Fruit Technology were added.
Area: The total area of the Regional
Station at present is 32 acres. This Ming
inadequate, efforts arre in hand to acquire
more area in the vicinity. Nearly 16 acres
of forest land has just been transferred for
the extension of the station. In addition to
this, cases are in hand for acquisition of 45
acres more land. Temperate Fruit Research
Station at Kotkhai, with an area of 25 acres
will also serve as an out-station of the Regional Fruit Research Station. With the
acquisition of more land, the total area of
the Regional Fruit Research Station is expected to be in the neighbourhooq. of 93
acres.
Equipment: The laboratories of different
sectio_llS of the Research Station are furnished with essential equipmerit arid these facilities are being developed further.
Laboratory B'Iltildings: There is a threeroom,ed fielcl laQ9ratory i'\t the Station. A

new double storeyed laboratory building,
consisting of 12 rooms has recently been completed. Another new building, consisting of
4 big halls and 4 rooms is to be constructed.
This will house the auditJorum, library,
museum and some laboratories. A sum cif
Rs. 1,24,000 has already been sanctioned
for the purpose. The laboratories which are
at present housed in a rented building will
be shift.( Ii in the new building very shortly.
Glass House: At present, there is one
glass house and one pot house at the Research Station. Plans are already on tihe
move :for the construction of 'more glass
houses.
Library: Library facilities exist at the
station and these are being developed further g_radually. There are more than 400
books on different subjects available in the
library. Important scientific journals are
being obtained from within and outside the
country.
Meteorological Observatory: A meteorological observatory equipped with standard
self recording instruments has been set and
is being improved further.
Altitude, Soil and Climate: The Research
Station is located at an altitude of 7,500 ft.
above sea level. The soil is clayey loam to
clayey, fairly deep and with good clayey
sub-soil. It is slightly acidic, the PH being
about 6.5.
Generally about 55-60 inches of rainfall
is recorded an!llJally most of it being in July
to September. The highest temperature
during the year does not ordinarily exceed
29.4°C (85°F) in June and the minimum does
not generally go below 4°C (25°F). Snowfalls are experienced during December to
March, the average annual snowfall being
150 cms. (5 feet).
Programme of Work: The station was
started in 1953 to collect and try important
varieties. of te~perate fruits with the object
of selectmg SUItable ones, to find out suitable rootstocks of apple and to determine its
optimum manurial requirements.
At present there are six sections and the
programme ?f work has been expanded. It
mcludes beSIdes the work already in progress, the selection of suitable :rootstocks for
pear and cherry, pollination requirements of
appl~, pear and ch~rry, training and pruning
req~Irements o.f dIfferent ~arieties of apple
findmg ~ut sUIt~bl~ methods of vegetative
propagatIon of mdIgenous and exotic rootst~cks of apple, pear and
cherry, chilling reqUIrements of dIfferent varieties of apple and

20
setection and breeding of apple varieties
with better dessert and keeping quality. The
investigations on various aspects of major
insect-pests and dis~ases of these fruits
with a view to devise a suitable control
measureS' are also in progress. Work on the
use of growth regulators in rooting of cuttings of indigenous and exotic clonal rootstocks of apple, pear and cherry, thinning
of fruits etc. has also been tak~..n up recently.
Scheme far Training of Gardeners: This
scheme is also located at the Regional Fruit
Research Station, Mashobra. During the
Second Plan period some 235 Gardeners
were trained in the art of fruit culture aQd
ornamental gardening. Previously the duration of the course was 6 months and a stipend of Rs. 30 per month per trainee wag
given. During the Third- Plan the duration

of the, training has been increased to one
year and it includes training in vegetable
growing and apiculture besides fruit culture
and ornamental gardening. The stipend has
also been increased to Rs. 40 per month
per trainee.
Distribution of Fertilizers: The Department has opened 55 fertilizer d,epots in all
blocks in the district thus facilitating the'
supply of fertilizers to the cultivators at
their homes. Ammonium Sulphate, Superphosphate and Calcium Ammonium Nitrate
are supplied to the cultivators for increasing
production of food grains at all India pool
price by subsidising the cost of internal
transport from rail heads to the distribution
centres. In order to popularize the' use of
fertilizers, large number of fertilizer trials
are laid every year on the' cultivators holdi."\gs free of cost.

Fisheries
Before setting up of Fisheries Department
in 1950-51, there were no fisheries rules or
regulations governing the fisheries assess in
the erstwhile States. After the organisation
of the Fishemes Department and with the
application of India Fisheries Act PI 1897
and Punjab Fisheries Act II 1914 and rules
fra~ed tbereunder, much of the evils to
whlch the fisheries of the area were sub,ec~

have been mended' and strides have been
made to place fisheries on firm footing. The
fishing has been now broughl, un~er a
rational licensing system and old methods of
indiscriminate and wanton killing of fish
viz. Poisioning, dynamiting have been prohibited. In the Pabar river in Rohru Valley
trout has been given due protection and a
hatchery has been set up at Chergaon to
fully stock trout in ?abar river.
To suit the administrativ~ convenience/ redistribu.tio):l of jurisdictioIl· between ,Assist;ant Ward on of Fisheries, Mahasu and Bilaspur was done in the year 1956 and Sutlej
ca~hrnalt area upto Seoni was braught
under the control of Assistant Wardon of
Fisheries, fJHaspur. In the lower ~at9hment
area the pond culture has received considerable :l.ttenUon.

The waters of the district can be divided
into two categories, namely trout waters and
waters other than trout waters.
Trout: The Pabar river in Rohru Valley
abounds with trout (Salmo fario) where one
can catch trouts of considerable size. It is
in all 30 miles in length, out of which 15
miles is a special reserved for '.Trout Anglers'. Baspa river in Sangla Valley has also
quality sizes trout; but due to its remoteness and lack of comIl).unication, it 'is still
unknown to the outside world of its beautiful treasurt;!. A smalL trout hatchery unit at
Chergaon is maintained by.the department
to cater to the trout popula'tion in the rivel
Pabar.

(e) Feed and Fodder Development;_ An

can be largely negatived if the animals are

increase of 30 per cent in milk pro,duction of
cows.
The supply of green fodder so' necessary
for the healthy up-keep of cattle and milch
cows, is not only meagre but erratic. It is
also 'a recognised fact that wHhout proper
feeding the inherited qualities are oot properly_ manifested in the .off spring, no matter
how-so-ever the superior germ-plasm be introduced amongst the progeny, .All the
breeding programme' will not bring substantial results unless adequate arrange'ments for tpeir feeding is made. In order to
improve upon the pastures a. scheme namely

Panchayats
There was no regular system of Panchayat
in the erstwhile princely States except the
area of Kotgarh and Kotkhai where twe,ntytwo Panchayats were functioning under the
Punjab Panchayat Raj Act, 1939. There were
3 Panchayats in Baghal, 7 in Bhajji, 27 in
Jubbal, 4 in Kumhar.sain and 4 in Baghat
State. These indigenous Panchayats were
organised either for one village or for a
group of villages. The functions of these'
Panchayats were confined only to village administration and other works in respect of
the uplift of the villages.
In 1949 Punjab Panchayat Raj Act, 1939
was extended to Himachal Pradesh and the
Panchayat Raj of respective princely State
was repealed. These Panchayats were to perform certain civic as well as 'judicial functions without any r.eservation of seats for
women or Scheduled Castes till their abolition on the 31st July, 1953.
The 'Himachal Pradesh Pahchayat Raj Act
was passed in 1952. Under this Act, the
principle of election to Gram Panchayats on
adults suffrage consisting of all adults ordinarily residing within its jurisdiction, ,vas
accepted. 152 Gram Panchayats one in each
Patwar circle covering the whole rural area
of the district were established in 1954. A
special feature of the system of election was
the reservation of seats for women and Scheduled Castes.
The Gram Panchayats were assigned only
executive functions. In addition to general
administrative apd IT!unicipal functions, certain duties concerning to development works
were made the responsibilities of the Gram
Panchayats under the Panchayats Raj Act
and thr~e tier structure was envisaged comprising '0£ Gram Panchayats, Tehsil Panch ayats and 'Zila Panchayats, on the enforcement of Himachal: Prad~Slh T(!rritorial Act,
1957 and the .emergency of the Territorial
Counci~ after th'e conversion of Himachal
Pradesh from part 'C' State into centrally
Administrative Union Territory and the
abolition of the legislature, the Zila
Panchayats were abolished because the
powers and functions of these bodies were
transferred to the Territorial. Council.

were completed in, 1957. Elections of Panches
to Nyaya Panchayats were also held. 142

At district level Zila Parishad, an ad hoc
body, has been constituted ~or the district
which has replaced district Development and
Planning Advisory Committee and tehsil
Panchayats have been entrusted the functions of Block Development Committees.
The Himachal Pradesh Panchayat Haj Act
provides for the establishment of conciliation boards or Samjhauta Samities in each
Gram Sabha. A Samjhauta Samiti is constituted by the President of the Gram Panchayats comprising of neither more than five
nor Jess than three members of the Panchayat including the President to conciliate
petty cases through amicable settlement
between the parties. The object of conciliation board is to offer opportunity to the parties concerned to make amicable settlements
of their disputes and criminal cases before
they go to the Nyaya Panchayats. These conciliation boards try to bring the parties to an
agreed settlement within a period of three
months from the date of filing of an application for compromise.

Organisation and Structure: The basic unit

i,n the organisation and sitructure of the Pan-

chayats is the Gram Sabha which means the
entire adult population of the territorial
limits fixed by notification for e1ach Gram
Sabha Adult under the Panchayatsl law
means, every male and female who has completed 21 years age.

Every Gram Sabha elects the executive
body, namely the Gram Panchayat, and also
the judicial one viz. the Nyaya Panchayat,
for its area. In the Gram Panchayat a CE'rtain number of seats is reserved for the Scheduled -Castes and the women, though the
'electorate is joint. The system of election
is based in adult franchise. The number of
the members of a Gram Panchayat varies
between 7 and 15 according to the population in addition to the President and the
Vice-President.
A Nyaya Panchayat consists of 15 PanchE's,
of whom at least 1/5 should be able to record proceedings in Hindi. The term of office
of every member of the Gram Panchayat as
well as the Nyaya Panchayat is three years.
The term of Gram Panchayal can be further
extended under the order of administration_
For each tehsil and sub-tehsil, there is a
'rehsil P anchay at. The number of the members varies from 10 tGl 40. The Tehsil Panch ayat is constituted of members appointed by
the State Government either by name or
by official designation, and of elected metl1bers.
The term of office of the members of the
Tehsil Panchayats is also three years.
Every Gram Panchayat has a whole time
Secretary, who maintains the records of the
Gram Panchayat as well as the Nyaya Panchayat.
The Secretaries are given' intensive training on various subjects connected with their
duties.
Every Gram Panchayat has a Chowkidar.
who also acts as process server, the messenger, and the general functionary at the
lowest rung even in develop men t activities
of the Gram Panchayat.

Powers and Duties: The compulsory duties
of the Panchayat include the construction,
repair, maintenance and lighting of public
street, medical relief, sanitation. up-keeps
protection and supervision of any building
or other property pertaining to the Gram
Panchayat, registration of births~ deaths
and marriages, public places and property
vested in the Gram Sabha ,establishment' management and care of common grazing
grounds and land for the common benefit,
taking steps ·to ,prevent fire, maintenance and
control of waste water, maintenance Q1f all
such roads and water courses the management of which has been undertaken by the

26
Panchayat with the sanction of the
Government.

The -Gram Panchayat can make any re.commendations to the grant of trees for construction of house, fuel, grant of a loan or
subsidy, for economic betterment, gran~ of
a license for possessing of fire arm and for
shooti!ig, grant of a nautor land for cultivation to an applicant residing within the
jurisdiction of such Gram Panchayat. Besides these the Panchayats are free to take
up works designed to promote the uplift
of the villagers.
Moreover, the Panchayats are the executing agency of many development works
done in their areas. It has been decided that
small works like construction of school
buildings, kubIs, bowlies etc. should be executed through Panchayats and not through
contractors. In order to get maximum possible cooperation from the public it has been
decided that small irrigation works, like construction of irrigation channels and kuhls,
which does not exceed Rs. 10,000 in value
should be executed through Panchayats.
The Administration has, further, taken the
following steps to make these bodies effective:1. All heads of departments in the Ad-

ministration have been requested to
give due weight to the recommendations of Panchayats.
2. Supervision of supply of foodgrains
in 1:he Territory has been entrusted to
Panchayats.
3. Distribution of timber is made through
the Panchayats.
4. Nautor lands are granted generally
on the recommendations of Panchayats.

Security jor keeping peace: Nyaya Panchayats have powers. to take security for
keeping peace. They have exclusive cognizance over certain offences which have been
precluded from the jurisdiction of the court.
The appearance of lawyers before Nyaya
Panchayats is forbidden by law in order to
save simple people of the villages from burdensome payments of fees to the lawyers.
For hearing and trial of a_ case, suit and
proceeding, a bench of five Pp.n,ches is constituted and the opinion of the majority prevails. The Act pI;ovides for an opportunity
for any aggrieved person to .fil~ an appeal
before the full bench of the Panchayat. An
application for revision can also be filed in
the court of the Sub-Divisional Judge/Magistrate.

Financial Resources: The financial resources of the Panchayats are very limited. They
.get nominal local rates 'as well as income
from Samjhauta cases. The Government
give grant to meet the expenses on account
of pay of Secretary and Chowkidar.

Co-opet:ative Movement
The Co-operative. movement i,lJ. this district
originated from the marketipg of potatoes in
the year 1945 when the then, Political Agen1
for Simla Hills Mr Bazelgette organised
about six Zamindaras Association in the
States. These Associatio,lJ.s were organised to
ensure supplies of potatoes to the British
Forces stationed in India due to the exige:ncies of Second World War and were registered under different laws in force in
those princely States. It was only after the
formation of Himachal Pradesh on the 15th
of April, 1948 when the Co-operative Act of
1942 was extended to this territory that the
Co-operative movement in real sense, was
started in the district. The old Zamindara
Associations were brought i.n the fold of cooperation and multi-purpose co-operative
societies were organized from the year 1949
onwards. In addition to these societies', some
societies were inherited from Kotgarh and
Kotkhai area of Punjab on their transfer to
this Pradesh.

The most effective measure for the economic emancipation of the agriculturists would
have been the organisation and setting up of
large-scale industries which could divert a
substantial proportion of the population from
agriculture to industry. But owing to t~e conditions peculiar to the district chances for
starting large-scale industries in the near
future are very dim. This district though
rich in forest, mineral, animal and horticultural resources has two relatively well-established industrial units namely Dyer Meakin Breweries Ltd., Solon and Kasauli Distillery, Kasauli. The district has great potentialities. in the shape of raw material for the
establishment of cottage and small scale industry. These industr1eSl go a long way to supRlement the income of many, besides being
ancillaries to large scale industries. Such
development would 'envisage the extension
of work opportunities, raising of incomes and
thereby the standard of living of the people
and to bri~g about a more balanced and integrated rural economy. A start was given to
this programme during the First Five Year
Plan with the objects of:(i) Utilising the raw materials available
locally;·
(ii) Providing employment and thereby
improving the economic condition
of the people, especially in the rural
areas; and

(iii) Increasing the production potential
for meeting the basic needs of the
people.

Blacksmithy: The Lahars are important
village artisans who, more or less, are indispensable. Lohar community of the villages
is engaged in the household industries of
making agricultural implements, certain
mjnor utensils, ornaments and tools. They
carry out repairs and mend old implements
for which payment is made in kind. Almost
a Lahar has fixed perquisites, depending upon
the number of ploughs and bighas of land
held by the household concerned. On festivals
and marriages he is served with free meals.
There is no elaborate workshop and the furnace is fixed in one corner outside the house.
There are two blacksmithy training centres
one is at Rohru and other at Solon. The
Rohru Centre was opelled in 1960. From 1960
to 1963 it trained 16 trai.nees. During 1962-63
this centre produced_ goods worth Rs. 2,271.56
and earned a profit of Rs. 1,420.
'Blacksmithy Centre Solon is located in the
Industrial Estate Solon. It was established
in 1962. The aim 'of this centre is to render
necessary help of blacksmithy to the different factories located in ·the Estate.
Basketry: Bamboo utensils is .a necessity
for the agriculturists. The articles prepared
out of bamboo are required by the villagers
for their day-to-day use. Men carry agricultural produce, vegetable, pots full of water
and cow-dung in Kiltas while women use
small and big size baskets. Utensils of bamboo are helpful for storing grains and flour
and distributing cooked things at the time
of festives The Barars, Bhanjaras, Dumnas,
Kalis and Rehars are engaged in basketry
but this is their subsidiary occupation. For
raw materials they depend on the forest produce like bamboo and grass reeds. The craftsmen are paid a share in crop at the time of
harvest. Under the scheme of imparting
training to artisans and reviving this old art
and giving new touch a Basket-ware Training Cell tre, Brotiwala was established
in 1958. According to a sanctioned strength
this centre enrols ten apprentices for a complete course of one year. For the first four
months each trai.nee is paid a stipend of
Rs. 30 per month, In the next four months
stipend is reduced to Rs. 20 per month plus
wages calculated on the basis of daily output. In the la8lt four months the stipend is
further reduced to Rs. 15 per month plus
wages.
Carpentry: Carpenters prepare agricultural implements. Industries d~partment started wood working cehtres at Jubbai in 1953

and at Chaupal in 1956. FOIl a full course of
one year each trainee gets a stipend of Rs. 30
per month for the first four months. In the
next four months this stipend is reduced to
RSI. 20 per month plus wages worked out on
daily output. In the- last four months the stipend is further reduced to Rs. 15 per month
plus wages.
Under the programme of rural arts and
crafts in the Community Development
Blocks, :rainees are provided improved tools
ani implements on 50 per cent subsidised
ra tes from the block funds.
The aim of ttle Training Centre is to impart traIning and to afford common facilities
to the local artisans ..
Leather Work: The cobblers carry out
their common hereditary profession. 1'hough
their profession offers better ptospects yet
they work as agriculturists on tiny un-economic holdings. They prep air and repair shoes
to meet the demand of local zamindars in
return of their customary wages in kind at
the time of harveslt. ,Shoemakers in the
urban areas are fully' occupied throughout
the year.
Tanning is carried on by the local shoe..
makers as a part time occupation. The leather
tanned by them is mostly used for their own
use. Leather tanning industry has not been
developed on proper lines. Old and out dated
methods are still in use. The known methods
of fiayings, salting, and tanning are crude.
Now t~ernment has established TanI ning Centre at Arki and Dhami.
Pottery: Pottery relics are often the only
evidence of by gone civilisations. The potter
fulfills the daily needs of village folk. All
goods are prepared from clay and a type of
special clay is gen,erally prepared. Sometimes the products are baked that gives a
sort of blackish touch. Goods in clay contain water, pickles, foodgrains, oil, milk,
and ghee. These utensils are common featUJ;'es of every r"lral household. Chilam
made of clay for smoking is very popular.
Once a while the potters prepared Khaprails.
These are house tiles used for roofing.

Weaving: Weaving is practised since time
immemorial to cater to the local needs. Many
agriculturists in upper Mahasu make woollen clothes for their own use. Different varieties of woollen articles such as pattus, p'attis,
blankets, tweeds, shawls and mufflers are
produced in the district. The productivitj[ of
the workers is low because they work on pitlooms with throw shuttles. Bushahri woollen
caps, chaddars, and' blankets are quite famous.
Government has distributed some looms
among villagers. Weaving Training Centres
have been opened at Rarppur and Rohru.
Dyer Meakin Breweries Limited Solon:
This Company traces its history back to the
year 1853, when a bre.wery was set up at
Kasauli by Mr. Edward Dyer of Messers. K
Dyer & Co. This firm was partnered by the
brothers, E. 'Dyer and E.J.R. Dyer, who also

promoted a private company under the name
and style of the Amritsar Distillary Company in the year 1898. Mr. Edward Dyer
was the brewing pioneer 1n India, and he
set up Breweries at Simla, Solon, Lucknow
and at Mandaly in Burma.
During the same century, another enterprising gentleman, named H.G. Meakin, who
·came from a well known brewing family of
Burton-on~Trent, founded Meakin & Co. lIe
bought the Simla and Kasauli breweries and
built others at Dalhousie, Ranikhet, Chakrata,
Darjeeling and Kirkee.
The object of these two firms was·to supply
cask beer to the British soldiers stationed at
these places and at cantonment towns situated within conveni~nt distribution range.
Both the firms E. Dyer & Co. and Meakin
and Co. continued their activities separately
until after the seeond decade of the 20th
century. During the First World War (191418), when it became somewhat problematical
to import sUfficient quantities of beer into the
country, these two firms rose to the occasion
and supplied large quantities of this beverage to the British soldiers resident in Lndia
,md to the other beer drinking public at
reasonable prices. A fairly large quantity of
beer went overseas also. Apart from beer,
Jarge quantities of barley malt, processrd at
the maltings of these firms, were sent to
Egypt, with a view to enabling the breweries
in that country to supply beer to soldiers (It
rEasonable prices.
In operation along with additional plant
installed there. The distillery building at
Solon Brewery was demolished. In its place
now stands a tall, spacious building, which
was constructed to house the new, modern
brewing equipment and plant and maohinery.
Kasauli Distillery, Kasauli (H.P.) and Dyer
Meakin Breweries Limited Solon are the
large-scale units in the district which are
engaged in the production of alcoholic beverages such as beer, malta whisky and spirit.
The products of these units are marketed
throughout the country.

Employment Service: The National Employment Service in India, as we alI know, is
the product of post-war demobilization. A
large number of service personnel and warworkers who were to be released had to be
resettled in civil life. Considering the complexity of the problem, the Directorate General of Resettlement and Employment (Government of India) was established in July,
1945, and Employment Exchanges were gradu~lly set up. In 1947, the colossal problem
created by the rehabilitation of the refugeeS!

from Pakistan res.ulted in the extension of facilities offered by the Employment Service to
the Refugees and by the 1948, the facilities
were thrown open to all categories of workers in response to growing demands on it.
In November, 1956, Himachal Pra~sh Government took over from the Central Governmen t the only Employment Exchange in the
Pradesh at Mandi a,nd with that was set up
the DiTectorate of Employment. The ~xchange for the Mahasu District was established at Solon on November:, 1960, with a Sub'ofiice Employment Exchange at RampuF: In
addition, four Employment Information and
Assistance Bureau WCL'e set up at Chaupal,
Jubbal, Kunihar, ana Theog.

Duration of Training: The duration of
training for engineering trades is 2 years
(H years institutional followed by 6 months
in plant 1 apprenticeship training in factory
or workshop). For Non-engineering trades
the training period is only one year, institu·tional.
•

Prospects for Passed-out Trainees: As has
been stated earlier, the training equip young
men for setting up their own :work. It does
not guarantee service to them, though every
effort is made by the Employment Exchanges to find the trainees gainful employment
in industries.

Qualifications for Admissions: For Draftsmen (Ciyjl). Electrician, Surveyor, Radio
Mechanic Stenography (English/Hindi) is
Matriculation or equivalent. For the remaining trades educational qualification is upto
Middle School standard (relaxable in suitable cases). Candidates between 16 to 25
years of age are normally admitted for training but the upper age-limit is relaxable for
ex-servicemen, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes candidates,. bonafide displaced
goldsmiths and their children, and in other
deserving cases.

Scheduled Tribes-5 per cent.
Bonafide Displaced Goldsmiths and their
Children-5 per cent.
Women (for stenographY)-25 per cent.
Ol'phan-2 per cent.

Marketing Practices: The producers generally bring their produce to the markets near
the road heads where the assembling and distribution cperations are carried on. In Mahasu
potato is th~ most important single cash crop.
Kotgarh and Kotkhai are the lands of apples.
Apples are sold by the owners in the
orchards and the buyers themselves arrange
for transportation. Apples are classified into
varieties and prices are settled according to
the size and variety of the apples. The seed
potatoes which are mostly exported to all
states are graded and sized in a loose customary manner.

Land Reforms: (i) In view of the small
holdings, the rt"lations between the landlords and tenants are generally cordial. Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, has provided relief to the
te~ants. as. 'they are eJigible to acquire propnetary nghts of the land under their
tenancy. This measure has no doubt safeguarded the int~rests of the te'P-an~ cl?!?s,

There are three kinds of land tenures prevalent in the Pradesh. These are:-

1. Zamindari

2, Pattidari

3. Baichara

(a) Perfect or Mukkammil..
(b) Imperfect Or Gairmukkammil.
(a) Perfect or Mukkammil.
(b) Imperfect or Gairmukkammil.

Zamindari system of lan_9 tenures are thosE.'
which are either owned by a single proprietor or jointly by more than one. Pattidari are
those in v.hich each proprietor owns not the
particular fields which he cultivates, but a
specific ancestral share in the whole estate.
Perfect or Mukkammil Pattidari tenures are
those in which all the lands are divided and
held in severally among the different proprietors in proportion to ancestral or other customary share in the revenue paid. All the cosharers are jointly responsible in the event
anyone among them failSi to fulfil his obligations or liabilities to the government, Imperfect or Gairmukkammil Pattidari tenures
are those in which part of the land is held
in sev.erally and part on community. The
interests of the land owners in: bQtll Gone;;pond to t~~ cus~o~iry shares,

38
In Bhaichara system of land tenue, every
man is the owner of only as much land as is
in his possession or as it is commonly' put
possession .is the measure of rights' in such
system. In perfect Bhaichara tenures, all the
lands are held in severally b)lt customary
shares. if they ever existed, have disappeared.
Each holding or rather the 'portion of total
revanue which a land owner 'pays has become
the sole measure of his rights and liabilities.
An imperfect Bhaichara differs from a perfect Bhaichara system in exactly the same
mann'er as an imperfect Pattidari differs
from a perfect Pattidari estate.

Naldera: Mashobra and Naldera are two

very important picnic spots on the SimlaTattapani road· About twenty Kilometres
from Simla motor road is the Naldera golf
course. The nine-hole course is very popular
with the golf-enthusiasts. It is famous for its

the two-room tourist hut or in the P.W.D.
rest how,!:!.
Narkanda: Surrounded
by magnificent
forests, Narkanda lies 9,000 feet above sea
level and J3 miles from Simla. This is a
ramous tourist centre. A favourite picnic spot
here is the Hattu Peak, 10,300 feet high. This
is a good place for outing, and commands a
unique view of the enternal snowline and the
dense forest full of both bi.e: and small game.
There are merry delightful walks. The five
set rest house has all the modern facility,
radio. books and indoor games.
Rampur: Rampur is situated on the left
bank of the Sutlej at an elevation of 3,500
feetl 1at. Jl"27' and long 77a41~. The town
is surrounded by cliffs which confine the air

and render the plaCe very hot in summer.
'This is a well known trade centre where a
number of down country merchants havp.
shops. Lavi the biggest trade lair in Hima("hal is held there in the second week of
November every year which attracts thousands of people and traders from far off
places. This is famous for shawls, chaddars,
chilgoza and ponies. There is an ancient
Tibetan temple with gigantic prayer wheels
and a temple dedicated to Lord Shiva. There
is a college, a high school, a civil hospital, a
rest h01)!';e, a sub-post office, a telegraph
office and a pOlice station.

Rohru: It is about 88 miles north of Simla
accessible by bus. The Pabar river in Rohru

Satogra: Salogra is situated 27 miles

Sarahan: This place is 27 miles north of
Rampur and 7,246 feet higher above the sea
levels lat. 31 °30', long. 77°50' on the old Hmdustan-Tibet road. Its site is fine, being 1IJ
'a beautifully wooded recess formed by the

Solon: Solon a popular summer resort.
lies midway between Kalka and Sirpla. It IS
connected with both by rail and road. ThIS

first class, higher secondary school, training college, a civil hospital and a post office.

PART tv

VILLAGE DIRECTORY

365-366

]JXPLANATORY NOTE TO VILLAGE Di:&1i1dTORY
The Village Directory renders an accouht
of each village and town in the district.
It gives the location code number, name of
each Village, area in acres, number of occupied residential houses, number of households,. ,total population and its break up by
sex, lIteracy, scheduled castes, scheduled
tribes, w'orkers and non-workers. The
figures (ilf workers are further split up by
sex and by a broad classification of industrial activity in nine categories.
2. In the village directory, the villages
arc presented tehsilwise. The villages have
been arranged in the ascending order of
their location code numbers. These\ code
numQers had been assigned to them for
organizing '1961 Census work and follow a
regular hadbast number. An alphabetical
list of villages will be found facing each
tehsil. It shows'the c.ode and hac\bast number of -each village. This will facilitate
location of any village in the village directory
as well as on 'the :spot.
3. A village having no population of Forest
villages have been shown with t}1e words
"uninhabited" against them.
4. Survey of India maps, previous Census
Handbooks and many other official sources
have been taken into' consideration to secure
accurate coverage and to get the correct
spellings of village names.
5. In Himachal Pradesh urban areas or
towns are places which either have a
Municipality or Small Town Committee or
Notified Area Committee. Census figures
for all these towns ar-e presented town-wise
after the completion of rural portion.
6. The village figures have extracted
directly from Census records. The figures

prensented in the village directory tally with
the tehsil and district Census tables perfectly.
7. Information contained in column (2)
immediately after the village n.ame is based
on the information supplied by the various
departments concerned. The symbols indicate the general pattern of distribution
of some basic amenities within village or
town. There were more useful items of
information on the villages which could not
be presented in the village directory for
want of space. The only important symbols
have been shown in the village directory.
8. The area figures in column (3) have
been 0 btained from the Director of Land
Records.
9. In column (4) of the village directory,
the occupied houses include houses used as
dwellings or partly as dwellings and partly
for some other purposes e. g. shop-cumdwellings.
10. Columns (9 to 12) of the village
directory present, for the first time, villagewise figures of population of Scheduled
Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
11. For columns (13) and (14) a "literate"
is a person who knows both reading and
writing.
12. The villagewise figures for industries
have been presented in a separate table
showing their industrial code number and
number of units in brackets. A list of Cooperative Societies, tables showing famous
temples or places of religiqus importance and
fairs and festivals have been given at the
end of this directory.
